title: Mutual Induction Between Two Coaxial Coils: Effect of Induced Current on the Voltage Across a Finite-Resistance Coil
description:
Two coils, (C_1) and (C_2), are placed coaxially with their axes aligned. The upper coil (C_1) is connected in series with an ideal battery of emf (V_1) and initially carries a steady current (I_1). Coil (C_1) has a finite resistance (R), and a voltmeter is connected directly across the two terminals of (C_1) to measure the voltage drop across the coil.

The lower coil (C_2) is connected to another ideal battery (V_2) through an initially open switch (S). When the switch (S) is closed, the current (I_2) in (C_2) starts increasing from zero. This changing current produces a changing magnetic flux through coil (C_1), thereby inducing an emf and an additional current in (C_1).

Assume that the induced current in (C_1) is in the same direction as the existing current (I_1). Consequently, the total current through (C_1) temporarily increases while the current in (C_2) is changing.

Determine and explain:

What happens to the total current through coil (C_1) immediately after switch (S) is closed?
Since (C_1) has finite resistance (R), what happens to the resistive voltage drop (IR) across (C_1)?
What voltage does the voltmeter connected across the terminals of (C_1) measure during this transient period?
Does the voltage across the coil necessarily remain equal to the ideal battery emf (V_1), or can it differ while the magnetic flux through (C_1) is changing?
After the current in (C_2) reaches a steady value and its magnetic flux through (C_1) stops changing, what happens to the induced emf and the voltmeter reading?

title: Why Does the Measured Voltage Differ Between Star and Open-Delta Connections?
description: If each transformer winding is rated at 230 V, why does the voltmeter show approximately 400 V when measuring between two line terminals in the star (Y) connection, while it shows only 230 V when measuring across the open winding of the delta (Δ) connection? Both arrangements appear to have two windings involved between the measuring points. What causes this difference in voltage?

title: Induced Current During Magnet Motion
description: A permanent magnet approaching a conducting coil changes the magnetic flux through the coil, producing an induced EMF and current. If the magnet stops briefly, the induced EMF falls to zero because the flux is no longer changing. When the magnet reverses direction, the current reverses as well according to Faraday's law and Lenz's law.

title: Diode Rectification in a Solenoid Experiment
description: Two magnets move toward a solenoid from opposite ends while the terminals form a loop containing an ideal diode. The diode changes this behavior by allowing current during only one polarity of the induced voltage, making the mechanical response asymmetric.

title: Practical Electronics Bench Notes
description: Reliable hardware begins with careful observation. Measurements, wiring checks, and repeatable tests help connect circuit theory with real behavior. Documenting each experiment as a small, dated article makes it easier to compare results and improve the next prototype.
